docs.title: Wiring and settings
docs.text:
• Signals travel on their own kind of wire. Connect parts with the Connect Tool, the same as logic.
  • Every signal part adds up all the signals wired into it (up to 8), and can feed up to 32 other parts.
  • The whole chain reacts in the same tick the encoder sees a tilt, so there's no lag however long your chain is. If you wire a loop, the looped part reads its value from the tick before.
  • Look at any signal part to see its output and settings.
  • Use (E) steps a setting up, Tinker steps it down. Crouch to change a part's second setting.
  • Settings are saved with the part.

docs.title: Gyro Flywheel (1x1, 3x3, 5x5)
docs.text:
A heavy flywheel that spins on Inverter power and keeps its axle upright (whichever end is already up). It's your steady reference for Angle Encoders.

1x1 3x3 5x5 Size (blocks) 1 × 1 × 1 3 × 3 × 3 5 × 5 × 5 Weight ~50 kg ~110 kg ~250 kg Good for small, light rings medium rings big or heavy rings Value Spin-up 6 s from stopped to full Coast-down 10 s once power stops Holding at full spin, cancels 60% of the gimbal's unwanted turning every tick Power 1 charge per 6 in-game hours of running (a quarter of a day), from an Inverter Wire from 1 Inverter (power) Wire into up to 4 Angle Encoders
  • It must hang in a gimbal. It only steadies the body it's built on. Hang it in two bearings at right angles, both horizontal, so the craft can tilt around it.
  • Keep the inner ring small. If the flywheel's body has more than 60 parts it gives up with "Can't hold this much - mount it on a small gimbal ring". Bolted straight onto a craft, it won't hold anything.
  • Light, balanced rings level fastest. Heavy rings make it slow. Past about 15 times its own weight, it warns "Rings too heavy for this flywheel - use a bigger flywheel or lighter rings". Bigger flywheels level faster in heavier rings.
  • Like a real gyro, it doesn't resist turning around its own axle.
  • Its stored charge only keeps it spinning while the Inverter is still wired in.

Look at it to see its spin and how fast the gimbal is turning, plus a status: Holding steady, Spinning up, Levelling (with how far the axle is off upright), Needs power: wire an Inverter into it, or No power.

docs.title: Angle Encoder
docs.text:
Outputs your craft's tilt in degrees, measured against a linked Gyro Flywheel. It measures twist around the direction its face points.

  • Use one per axis. Face it forwards to read roll, or sideways to read pitch. Don't point it straight up: that axis is the flywheel's own spin.
  • Build it on the craft, not on the gimbal, and wire the flywheel into it.
  • It sets itself to 0 when you first link it. Level the craft and press Use to set the current angle as level (0) any time.
  • Output runs from −180 to 180. Which way is positive follows the right-hand rule around its face direction. If a correction comes out backwards, add a Flip.

docs.title: Gain
docs.text:
Multiplies its signal. This is how hard to correct.

Setting Range Default Gain (Use = more, Tinker = less) ×0.05 to ×50, in preset steps ×1

docs.title: Rate
docs.text:
Outputs how fast its signal is changing, per second. Feed it a tilt and it tells you how fast the craft is swinging. Add that in through a Gain to brake corrections before they overshoot.

Setting Steps Default Smoothing (Use = smoother, Tinker = sharper) 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 90% 50%

docs.title: Mixer
docs.text: Adds together every signal wired into it. No settings.

docs.title: Flip
docs.text: Outputs minus its signal. The thruster on the opposite side of the craft needs the opposite correction. No settings.

docs.title: Clamp
docs.text:
Caps its signal at ± a limit, and turns anything inside the dead zone into 0.

Setting Steps Default Limit (Use / Tinker) ±1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 75, 90, 100 ±100 Dead zone (crouch + Use / Tinker) 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5 0

docs.title: Set Point
docs.text:
Outputs a fixed number you choose, from −100 to 100. Use it as the base throttle your craft needs to hover. Nothing can be wired into it.

Setting Step Default Value (Use = +, Tinker = −) 1, or 10 while crouching 0

docs.title: Throttle Thruster
docs.text:
Pushes with exactly its signal as a percent of full thrust. It pushes away from its nozzle, so point the nozzle down to lift.

Value Size 2 × 2 × 4 blocks Full thrust (signal 100) 8,000 N, enough to hold up about 800 kg Signal 0 to 100. Below 0 counts as 0, above 100 as 100 Power about 1 charge per 30 s at full thrust, less at lower throttle, from an Inverter Wire from an Inverter, signal parts, switches (up to 8 in all)
  • Arming switch (optional): wire in a switch or other logic. With any switch wired in, at least one must be on or the thruster won't fire.
  • Look at it to see its throttle and status: Firing, Idle, Switched off, Needs power: wire an Inverter into it or No power.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Draws up to 3 signals as a live graph floating above itself. Use it to watch your controller wobble while you tune.

  • Wiring order sets the colour: first red, second green, third blue.
  • Shows the last 2.4 seconds, on a graph about 1.5 m wide and 1 m tall that turns to face you.
  • It scales itself to fit, but never zooms in tighter than ±10.

docs.title: Carbon Pipes
docs.text: Very light, paintable carbon pipes for building gimbal rings. They fit and snap like the small metal pipes: Straight, Long (4 blocks), Bend, T and Cross. Light, balanced rings let a flywheel level fast.

docs.title: Worked example: a self-levelling hover platform
docs.text: This build keeps a square platform flat on four thrusters, one at each corner.

docs.title: 1. Power
docs.text: You need an Inverter fed from your batteries (see Power). In this build it powers 5 devices: the flywheel and four thrusters. Use an Inverter of a high enough level for that many outputs, or two Inverters.

docs.title: 2. The gimbal
docs.text:
1. Build a small inner ring of Carbon Pipes around a Gyro Flywheel with its axle pointing up, and fix the flywheel to it.
  2. Put the inner ring on a bearing inside a slightly bigger outer ring.
  3. Put the outer ring on a second bearing on the platform's frame, at right angles to the first. Both bearing axes must be horizontal.
  4. Wire the Inverter into the flywheel and wait about 6 seconds. It should say Holding steady.

Tip

Keep the flywheel and inner ring under 60 parts, and keep both rings light and balanced. If it says the rings are too heavy, use a bigger flywheel or fewer pipes.

docs.title: 3. Sensing the tilt
docs.text:
1. Build two Angle Encoders on the platform itself, not on the rings:
    • a pitch encoder facing sideways
    • a roll encoder facing forwards
  2. Wire the flywheel into both.
  3. Park the platform level and press Use on each encoder to set 0.

docs.title: 4. The hover throttle
docs.text:
Work out the throttle your platform needs to just hover. With four thrusters, each one holds about 800 kg at full:

hover throttle ≈ platform weight ÷ (4 × 800 kg) × 100

A 1,200 kg platform needs about 1,200 ÷ 3,200 × 100 ≈ 38. Build a Set Point and set it to 38.

docs.title: 5. One correction per axis
docs.text:
For pitch:

  1. Pitch encoder → Gain (start at ×2). This is the push back toward level.
  2. Pitch encoder → Rate → Gain (start at ×0.5). This brakes the swing so it doesn't overshoot.
  3. Both Gains → a Mixer. That Mixer's output is your pitch correction.
  4. Pitch correction → a Flip, for the other end of the platform.

Build the same again for roll.

docs.title: 6. The four thrusters
docs.text:
Give each thruster its own Mixer (nozzle down, one at each corner), and wire in:

Thruster Set Point Pitch Roll Front left ✓ pitch correction roll correction Front right ✓ pitch correction flipped roll Back left ✓ flipped pitch roll correction Back right ✓ flipped pitch flipped roll

Wire each Mixer into its thruster, and the Inverter into every thruster.

docs.title: 7. Test and tune
docs.text:
1. Wire your Scope to the two encoders and one thruster's Mixer.
  2. Lift off and tip the platform a little. The encoder line should swing back to 0.
  3. Gets worse instead of better? That axis's correction is backwards. Swap which side gets the flipped signal (or add one more Flip on that axis).
  4. Slow to level? Raise the first Gain.
  5. Wobbles or overshoots? Raise the Gain after the Rate, or lower the first Gain.
  6. Twitchy at rest? Put a Clamp with a small dead zone after the encoder, or raise the Rate's smoothing.
  7. Sinks or climbs? Adjust the Set Point.

Add an off switch

Wire one switch into all four thrusters. While it's off, none of them fire, so the platform can sit on the ground with the controller live.

docs.title: Frontier Kitchen
docs.text:
The Frontier Kitchen turns the Cookbot into a cooking ladder. There are 35 Frontier dishes spread over five tiers: Classics, Campfire, Homestead, Expedition and Frontier Feast. Each tier heals more than the one below it and gives stronger buffs: health regeneration, damage resistance, deep breath (no running out of air underwater) and random perks. You start with the Classics. Cooking the dishes you know earns mastery, and you spend mastery to research the next tier's dishes at the Cookbot. Before you have a Cookbot, a Campfire built from scrap can cook the simple Classics. Some dishes can't be researched at all. The Traveling Trader sells those recipes, and they heal a little more and their buffs last longer.

At a glance

  • Five tiers: Classics, then Campfire, Homestead, Expedition and Frontier Feast. All dishes in a tier have the same stats. Only the ingredients differ.
  • Buffs: Regeneration (all tiers), Damage resistance (Homestead and up), Deep breath (Expedition and up), random perks (Expedition gives 1, Frontier Feast gives 2).
  • Research: collecting a cooked dish gives +1 mastery in its tier. Researching a dish costs 3 / 5 / 8 / 12 mastery from the tier below.
  • Shared by the party: mastery and researched recipes belong to the whole world. Buffs belong to each player.
  • Buffs don't stack. Eating again only replaces a buff that is weaker, or equally strong with less time left.
  • Campfire: crafted at the Workbench from 12 Scrap Wood and 4 Scrap Metal. It cooks the three Frontier Classics, one at a time.
  • /food shows your party's mastery, which dishes are researched and your active buffs.

docs.title: The five tiers
docs.text:
All dishes in a tier are equally strong. The table shows a dish you researched (or a Classic). Trader dishes are covered below.

Tier Heals Regeneration Damage resistance Deep breath Perks Classics 48 HP +1 HP/s for 15 s – – – Campfire 60 HP +1 HP/s for 30 s – – – Homestead 80 HP +2 HP/s for 40 s 15% for 3 min – – Expedition 92 HP +3 HP/s for 45 s 25% for 5 min 3 min 1 random perk Frontier Feast 98 HP +4 HP/s for 75 s 35% for 8 min 5 min 2 random perks

Here is how much health regeneration gives back over its full duration, if you are hurt the whole time: Classics 15, Campfire 30, Homestead 80, Expedition 135, Frontier Feast 300.

docs.title: What the buffs do
docs.text:
• Regeneration heals the listed amount once per second while you are conscious and below full health.
  • Damage resistance reduces all damage you take by the listed percentage.
  • Deep breath keeps your air full for its whole duration, so you can stay underwater without running out of breath.
  • Perks are the game's normal food perks. Each one is picked at random from those you don't have yet: Bonus Health (+25 max HP), Hammer Speed, Fall Protection and High Jump. When you already have all four, more perks do nothing.

Knocked out = buffs gone

Being knocked out removes all your food buffs and perks, including the +25 max HP from Bonus Health. A dish eaten while you are knocked out gives no buffs.

docs.title: Health is capped at 100
docs.text: Your maximum health is 100 HP, or 125 with the Bonus Health perk. Healing past your maximum is wasted. So above Homestead, the big jump between tiers is in the buffs, not the heal itself. The trader's Frontier Feast dishes heal 103, and the extra 3 only counts if Bonus Health has raised your maximum.

docs.title: Dishes by tier
docs.text:
Ingredients, cook times and which dishes are trader recipes are listed on the Dishes page.

Tier Researchable / always known Traveling Trader recipes Classics Baked Potato, Corn on the Cob, Grilled Fish, plus the game's own Pizza Burger, Veggie Burger and Revival Baguette – Campfire Tomato Soup, Corn Chowder, Mashed Potatoes, Carrot Soup, Cornbread, Milk Tea Trail Hash, Fish & Chips Homestead Steak & Mash, Berry Pancakes, Banana Bread, Root Stew, Pot Roast, Berry Banana Shake Shepherd's Pie, Borscht, Berry Cobbler Expedition Five-Alarm Chili, Tropical Smoothie, Broccoli Gratin, Fish Chowder, Smoked Pike Moonfin Curry, Smoked Eel Rolls, Orange-Glazed Steak Frontier Feast Ember-Seared Steak, Glow Risotto, Crystal Parfait, Sturgeon Feast Leviathan Steak, Ember Tarts, Crystal Sorbet

Campfire-tier ingredients all grow or turn up around the crash site. Every dish from Homestead up needs at least one ingredient that you only find farther out, so the kitchen keeps pulling you into new areas. Several dishes use fish or Fish Fillets from Fishing.

The game's own Classics

Pizza Burger, Veggie Burger and Revival Baguette sit in the Classics row and earn Classics mastery when cooked. They keep their normal effects, though, and give no Frontier buffs. The Frontier Classics (Baked Potato, Corn on the Cob, Grilled Fish) are the ones that give 48 HP and Regeneration.

Check the raid cost

Each dish's description in your inventory says what raid level you would trigger by planting the farmed crops for one cook. Use it to judge how big a farm a recipe really needs.

docs.title: Research and mastery
docs.text:
Cooking is how the kitchen levels up:

  1. Earn mastery. Each time you collect a finished dish from a Cookbot or Campfire, you get +1 mastery in that dish's tier. Mastery is counted per cook, not per item. A Campfire-tier recipe makes 2 dishes but still gives 1 mastery. If you collect several queued cooks at once, you get mastery for each of them.
  2. Spend it to research. Select a locked (dimmed) dish in the Cookbot window. Its description shows the research cost and how much mastery you have. The button reads Research (cost) and works once the tier below has enough mastery. Researching spends that mastery.
  3. Cook the new dish to earn mastery in its own tier, and so on up the ladder.

Each tier's cost is paid in mastery from the tier directly below it:

To research a... Costs Paid with Researchable dishes Cooks to research the whole tier Campfire dish 3 Classics mastery 6 18 Classics cooks Homestead dish 5 Campfire mastery 6 30 Campfire cooks Expedition dish 8 Homestead mastery 5 40 Homestead cooks Frontier Feast dish 12 Expedition mastery 4 48 Expedition cooks

Classics are always known and are never researched. Any dish in a tier counts toward that tier's mastery, so you can cook the cheapest recipe over and over.

Party-wide

Mastery and researched recipes are saved with the world and shared by everyone in it. Anyone can cook to add mastery, and anyone can spend it. When a dish is researched, everyone gets a chat message. Food buffs are personal: each player has their own.

docs.title: Trader dishes
docs.text:
Eleven dishes can't be researched. In the Cookbot they show as Traveling Trader recipes, and the button reads "At the Trader". Their recipes are sold on the Recipes tab of the Traveling Trader's Stall for Frontier Scrip. A tier's trader recipes go on sale once the party has researched at least one regular dish of that tier. After you buy one, the whole party can cook it at any Cookbot like any other dish, and cooking it earns mastery for its tier.

Trader dishes are a step up from the regular dishes in their tier:

  • Extra health: +5 HP over the tier's normal heal.
  • Buffs last 1.2x as long (rounded to the nearest second). Buff strength and perks are the same as the tier's.
Tier Recipe price Heals Regeneration Damage resistance Deep breath Perks Campfire 36 scrip 65 HP +1 HP/s for 36 s – – – Homestead 72 scrip 85 HP +2 HP/s for 48 s 15% for 3 min 36 s – – Expedition 80 scrip 97 HP +3 HP/s for 54 s 25% for 6 min 3 min 36 s 1 random perk Frontier Feast 192 scrip 103 HP +4 HP/s for 90 s 35% for 9 min 36 s 6 min 2 random perks

When you eat a trader dish, the message on screen calls it a "trader's special" instead of a "meal".

docs.title: The Cookbot window
docs.text:
The mod replaces the game's three-button Cookbot window with a grid of every dish. The Classics are on the first row, then one row per tier. Each row's label shows the tier and the party's current mastery in it, for example "Homestead - 7 mastery". Dishes you know are shown in full colour, and locked dishes are dimmed.

Selecting a dish shows its name, a 3D preview, its description, its ingredients and its cook time. The button changes with the dish:

Dish state Button Known, and you have the ingredients Craft Known, but ingredients are missing Craft (greyed out) Locked, researchable Research (3 / 5 / 8 / 12), active once you have enough mastery in the tier below Locked Traveling Trader recipe At the Trader (greyed out)

docs.title: All dishes / Cookable now
docs.text:
Two tabs at the top filter the grid:

  • All dishes shows every dish.
  • Cookable now shows only dishes you know and have every ingredient for, right now. Ingredients are counted from your own inventory plus every chest piped into the Cookbot, the same places the Cookbot takes them from when it cooks. The list updates about four times a second while the window is open, so it follows along as you fill chests or your inventory. In Creative mode (unlimited inventory), every known dish counts as cookable.

The tab you pick stays selected for every Cookbot until you leave the game.

docs.title: Cook times
docs.text:
The Cookbot cooks one order at a time.

Tier Cook time Dishes per cook Classics (Frontier) 10 s 1 Campfire 20 s 2 Homestead 30 s 1 Expedition 45 s 1 Frontier Feast 60 s 1

docs.title: The Campfire
docs.text:
The Campfire is how you start cooking before you have a Cookbot. Its recipe is known from the start.

Crafted at Workbench (in your crashed ship) Recipe 12 Scrap Wood + 4 Scrap Metal, 10 s Cooks The three Frontier Classics only: Baked Potato, Corn on the Cob, Grilled Fish Cook time 30 s per dish, one dish at a time Earns +1 Classics mastery per dish collected

To use it, press Use on the Campfire, pick a dish and press Craft. The fire burns while the dish cooks. When it's done, collect the dish from the process slot. If your inventory is full the dish stays on the fire and you get a warning.

Compared to the Cookbot, the Campfire:

  • Cooks only the Frontier Classics. It can't cook the game's own Classics or any higher tier.
  • Takes 30 s per dish instead of 10 s.
  • Uses only ingredients from your inventory, not from chests piped into it.
  • Has no research and no Cookable now tab.

Bank mastery early

Classics mastery earned at the Campfire is saved. Cook there while you work toward a Cookbot, and you can research your first Campfire-tier dishes as soon as it's built. At 3 mastery per dish, 18 Classics cooks research all six.

docs.title: Buff stacking and refresh
docs.text:
Food buffs don't stack. Each buff type (Regeneration, Damage resistance, Deep breath) is tracked on its own. When you eat, each buff the dish gives:

  • replaces your current buff of that type if the new one is stronger, or
  • replaces it if it is equally strong and lasts longer than the time you have left on the current one,
  • and is ignored otherwise.

What this means in practice:

  • Eating the same tier again refreshes your buffs to full duration.
  • A lower tier never overwrites a higher one. A Homestead dish won't cut short a Frontier Feast's 35% resistance.
  • A stronger buff always wins, even if it is shorter. Expedition's +3 HP/s for 45 s replaces Homestead's +2 HP/s however much time Homestead had left.
  • Expedition and Frontier Feast give the same Deep breath, so the longer one wins. A trader dish's longer buffs also win at equal strength.
  • Perks are always granted, whatever happened to the buffs.
  • If nothing changed, the on-screen message says "already well fed". You still get the health.

Buffs are saved with your character and keep counting down while you're in the game. When a buff runs out, a chat message tells you.

docs.title: HUD buff icons
docs.text:
Each active food buff shows as an icon in the status panel at the bottom left of the screen, after the game's perk icons. The order is always Regeneration, Damage resistance, Deep breath. Hover over an icon to see its strength and time left, for example "Damage resistance 25% - 4 min 12 s left". An icon shines once when you gain the buff or top it up, just like a new perk does, and it disappears when the buff runs out.

When you eat a Frontier dish, a message shows what you gained, for example "Expedition meal: Regeneration +3/s, Damage resistance 25%, Deep breath, 1 perk".

docs.title: The /food command
docs.text:
Type /food in chat for a full kitchen report:

  1. Cooking mastery: the party's current mastery in each tier.
  2. Every Frontier dish and its status: known, research for N mastery, or sold by the Traveling Trader for N scrip.
  3. Your food buffs: each active buff with its time left, or "No food buffs active".

    4. See Commands for the other chat commands.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text: What Shared or per player Mastery (all tiers) Shared by the whole party, saved with the world Researched recipes Shared. One research unlocks the dish for everyone Trader recipes bought Shared Food buffs and perks Per player "Cookable now" Counts your inventory plus the Cookbot's piped chests Campfire Cooks from the inventory of the player who starts the dish

docs.title: Dishes elsewhere
docs.text:
• Contracts: Supply Runs can ask for dishes of a tier, and contract rewards often include a few dishes.
  • Fishing: Fish Fillets and whole fish go into Grilled Fish, Fish Chowder, Smoked Pike, Sturgeon Feast and several trader dishes.
  • Full ingredient lists: Dishes. Other recipes: Recipes. All items: Items.

docs.title: Pipe Coupler
docs.text:
The Pipe Coupler joins two vacuum pipe networks that aren't built together, such as a lift platform and your base, or a supply truck and your factory. Pipe a coupler into each network and push their flat faces together. While they're docked, the two networks work as one: a Craftbot on one side uses the chests on the other side, pumps fill them, and items travel both ways. Pull the two sides apart and the networks are separate again.

At a glance

  • Size: 3 × 3 × 2 blocks. The pipe goes in at the back, and the flat face at the front is the docking face.
  • Docks when two couplers' flat faces touch, face to face. The lamps light up while docked.
  • Works both ways, and through chains of several docks.
  • Each side uses its own chests first, then the ones across the dock.
  • How to get it: a Traveling Trader blueprint (Common, 30 scrip, no reputation needed), then craft it at the Craftbot.

docs.title: Getting a Pipe Coupler
docs.text:
The recipe is a blueprint from the Traveling Trader. Buy it once and the whole party can craft couplers.

Blueprint Rarity Price Needs Pipe Coupler Common 30 Frontier Scrip nothing (Stranger reputation) Crafted at Ingredients Time Craftbot 20 × Metal Block, 2 × Circuit Board, 2 × Glue, 1 × Component Kit 15 s

Couplers stack up to 10.

docs.title: How docking works
docs.text:
1. On each network, build a coupler and connect a vacuum pipe to the opening at its back.
  2. Bring the two couplers together so their flat front faces touch, facing each other.
  3. When they're docked, both couplers' lamps light up. Look at one to see docked: pipes joined (or not docked).
Rule Value Faces must be within 0.2 m of each other (a few centimetres off still docks) Faces must point at each other (roughly face to face, not side by side or the same way round) Docking is noticed within a quarter of a second Undocking as soon as the faces move apart, or one coupler is removed

You can't build anything onto the flat docking face. It's kept clear so it can touch the other coupler.

Line them up

Moving one coupler a whole block out of line is enough to undock it. Guide rails or a stop block on your lift help it land in the same spot every time.

docs.title: What joins
docs.text:
While docked, anything on one network that uses vacuum pipes sees the containers on the other network too:

  • A Craftbot on one side lists and spends from the chests on the other side, and can put finished items into them.
  • Pumps on either side can fill the chests on the other side.
  • Item animations follow the pipes on both sides of the dock, so you can see items travelling through the couplers.

The join works both ways, and it chains. If network A docks with B, and B docks with C somewhere else, a Craftbot on A can use the chests on C.

Situation What happens The item is in a chest on your own side Your own chests are used first Your own chests are full Items overflow into the chests across the dock A chest is reachable two ways It's only counted once The item isn't anywhere on either side Nothing is spent, and the craft isn't queued

Note

Couplers only join pipe networks. Wires, power and logic aren't carried across a dock.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Lift platforms. Keep a chest on a lift platform and dock it against your base's pipes at the bottom. Your base Craftbots can use what's on the lift.
  • Supply vehicles. Put a coupler on the back of a truck that carries chests. Back it up to a coupler on your base and the factory can pull from the truck.
  • Separate buildings. Join two pipe networks on separate creations without welding them together.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The two couplers must be docked face to face. Couplers side by side or back to back don't join anything.
  • Each coupler follows up to 4,096 pipe pieces of its own network.
  • If you build or remove pipes on a docked network, the coupler picks up the change within about 5 seconds. Docking or undocking updates it straight away.
  • The Workbench has no pipes, so couplers make no difference to it.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Survival Frontier adds the first power source to Survival that makes energy instead of only storing it: solar. Solar Panels charge a Mega Battery Bank through a Charge Controller, and an Inverter turns the Bank's stored charge into power for the new devices: Floodlights, Chargers for Rechargeable Batteries, and Teleport Pads. Vanilla electric engines, drills and growbeds run straight off the Bank. Solar is slow and best at stationary outposts. Batteries stay the fast, portable option.

At a glance

  • The chain: Solar Panels > Charge Controller > Mega Battery Bank > Inverter > Floodlight / Charger / Teleport Pad.
  • Unit: 1 charge = 1 normal Battery. A Mega Battery holds 100, a Rechargeable Battery 25, a Bank 100.
  • Solar Panel: 15 charge per clear day, nothing at night, 15% of that in rain, nothing with anything above it.
  • Charge Controller: 5 levels, 2 / 4 / 6 / 10 / 16 panels.
  • Inverter: 5 levels, 2 / 4 / 6 / 8 / 10 devices at 80 / 85 / 90 / 93 / 96% efficiency.
  • Upgrades: Tinker, paid in Component Kits: 1 / 2 / 3 / 5 per step.
  • How to get them: all are Craftbot recipes unlocked by Traveling Trader blueprints.

docs.title: How power flows
docs.text:
Solar Panels ──► Charge Controller ──► Mega Battery Bank ──► Inverter ──► Floodlight / Charger / Teleport Pad
                                              │                          (also Gyro Flywheels, Throttle Thrusters)
                                              └──► electric engines, drills, growbeds (directly, like a battery container)
  • Wiring order is enforced. Each part only connects to the next one in the chain, and the connect tool only shows connection points on the right part. A wrong wire is removed, with a message such as "Solar Panels can only be wired into a Charge Controller".
  • Power is counted in charge. 1 charge is what one normal Battery holds.
  • The Inverter is only for the new devices. Vanilla machines don't need one: wire them straight from the Bank.

docs.title: Wiring limits
docs.text: Part Wire into it Wire out of it Solar Panel Nothing 1 Charge Controller Charge Controller Solar Panels (2 to 16, by level) Up to 4 Mega Battery Banks Mega Battery Bank Up to 4 Charge Controllers Inverters, electric engines, drills, growbeds Inverter Up to 4 Mega Battery Banks 2 to 10 devices, by level Charger Up to 2 Inverters Nothing Teleport Pad Up to 2 Inverters Nothing Floodlight Inverter (power) + switch, button or Light Sensor (on/off), 3 wires in total Nothing Light Sensor Nothing Up to 255 parts

docs.title: How to get them
docs.text:
Every part here is built in the Craftbot, but only after the party owns its blueprint from the Traveling Trader. A blueprint unlocks its recipe for the whole party. Rarer blueprints need more trader reputation.

Item Rarity Price Needs first Ingredients Craft time Solar Panel Uncommon 72 scrip - 6 Metal Blocks, 4 Glass Blocks, 1 Circuit Board 30 s Charge Controller Uncommon 72 scrip Solar Panel 1 Circuit Board, 2 Component Kits, 5 Metal Blocks 20 s Inverter Uncommon 72 scrip Solar Panel 2 Circuit Boards, 3 Component Kits, 10 Metal Blocks 30 s Mega Battery Rare 144 scrip - 100 Batteries, 2 Circuit Boards, 25 Metal Blocks, 25 Chemicals 30 s Mega Battery Bank Legendary 300 scrip Mega Battery 8 Metal Blocks, 1 Circuit Board, 2 Component Kits 30 s Rechargeable Battery (crafted Empty) Common 30 scrip - 2 Circuit Boards, 10 Metal Blocks, 5 Glow, 10 Chemicals 30 s Charger Uncommon 72 scrip Rechargeable Battery 2 Circuit Boards, 2 Component Kits, 8 Metal Blocks 20 s Floodlight Common 30 scrip - 1 Circuit Board, 4 Metal Blocks, 2 Glass Blocks 20 s Light Sensor Common 30 scrip - 1 Circuit Board, 2 Metal Blocks, 1 Glass Block 10 s

Only level 1 of the Charge Controller and Inverter is crafted. Higher levels come from upgrading. See also Recipes and Items.

docs.title: Solar Panel
docs.text:
Makes power from sunlight. Look at a panel to see its current output as a percentage and why ("Clear", "Cloudy", "Rain", "Night", "No open sky").

  • Clear day: 15 charge per panel per in-game day.
  • Daylight curve: output starts at 06:00, peaks at noon and stops at 18:00. Nothing at night.
  • Clouds: cut output by up to 75%, depending on how cloudy it is (never below 25%).
  • Rain: 15% of normal, about 2.25 charge per day.
  • Open sky: anything up to 80 m straight above the panel blocks it completely ("No open sky").
  • Angle: doesn't matter. Panels work on vehicles too.

A Solar Panel also counts as a power source for a powered Survey Post (see Contracts).

docs.title: Charge Controller
docs.text:
Collects the panels' output and charges Mega Battery Banks with it, one charge at a time. It fills the first wired Bank that has room, then the next. Look at it to see how many panels it's using and its charge per day right now. Press Tinker to upgrade.

Level Panels Clear-day output Cost to reach this level 1 2 30 charge (crafted) 2 4 60 charge 1 Component Kit 3 6 90 charge 2 Component Kits 4 10 150 charge 3 Component Kits 5 16 240 charge 5 Component Kits

Panels past the level's limit can't be wired in. When every wired Bank is full, the extra solar power is lost.

docs.title: Mega Battery Bank
docs.text:
Stores up to 100 charge. It has one battery slot for a Mega Battery (100 charge) or a charged Rechargeable Battery (25 charge). A gauge on the Bank ticks down as it's used.

  • Solar charging: a Charge Controller wired into it fills it up to 100. No battery has to be in the slot for that.
  • Loading a battery: a battery in the slot is loaded only if its charge fits (the Bank's charge plus the battery's charge can't go over 100). A Mega Battery only loads into an empty Bank.
  • Locked slot: while a battery's charge is in use, the slot is locked ("cell locked until drained").
  • Running out: when the Bank reaches 0, the battery in the slot is spent. A Mega Battery is used up. A Rechargeable Battery comes back Empty, ready for a Charger.
  • Outputs: wire it straight to electric engines, drills and growbeds like a vanilla battery container, or to an Inverter for the new devices.

Tip

A Bank on solar that never runs dry never spends the battery in its slot. The battery is the reserve for nights and rainy days.

docs.title: Mega Battery
docs.text: Holds as much power as 100 Batteries. It only fits in a Mega Battery Bank and is used up when drained. It also counts as a power source for a powered Survey Post.

docs.title: Inverter
docs.text:
Turns stored Bank power into the power the new devices run on: Floodlights, Chargers, Teleport Pads, Gyro Flywheels and Throttle Thrusters. It keeps a small buffer of 2 charge for its devices and refills it from the first wired Bank that has charge. Some energy is lost in converting. Look at it to see its efficiency, devices wired and total charge available. Press Tinker to upgrade.

Level Devices Efficiency Bank charge used per 1 device charge Cost to reach this level 1 2 80% 1.25 (crafted) 2 4 85% 1.18 1 Component Kit 3 6 90% 1.11 2 Component Kits 4 8 93% 1.08 3 Component Kits 5 10 96% 1.04 5 Component Kits

Warning

Electric engines, drills and growbeds don't go through an Inverter. Wire them from the Bank directly. An Inverter wired to anything other than its devices gets that wire removed.

docs.title: Rechargeable Battery
docs.text:
Holds 25 charge. It is crafted Empty, so charge it in a Charger first.

  1. Put the charged battery in a Mega Battery Bank's slot. It loads its 25 charge when that fits.
  2. When the Bank runs dry, the battery comes back Empty in the slot.
  3. Take it out, charge it in a Charger and use it again.

docs.title: Charger
docs.text:
Fills Empty Rechargeable Batteries using power from an Inverter. Press Use to open it.

  • Slots: 4. Only Rechargeable Batteries go in.
  • Speed: draws 1 charge per second while there's an Empty battery inside, so one battery takes 25 seconds. Batteries charge one at a time.
  • Progress is kept: the charge built up for the current battery is saved if power runs out.
  • Cost: 25 charge from the Inverter per battery, which is 31.25 Bank charge at level 1 and about 26 at level 5.

docs.title: Floodlight
docs.text:
A bright light for outposts. It needs two kinds of wire:

  • Power from an Inverter.
  • On/off from a switch, button, Light Sensor or other logic part. The Floodlight never decides by itself when it's dark.

It shines while any wired logic part is on. It uses 1 charge per 12 in-game hours of light, so a full night costs 1 charge. Look at it to see "On", "Off" or "No power".

docs.title: Light Sensor
docs.text:
A logic part that turns on when it's dark. Press Use to flip it to on when light, and again to flip it back.

  • It counts as dark while the sun is below 5% strength: from about 17:50 to about 06:10 in-game.
  • It works anywhere, covered or not. It only goes by the time of day.
  • Wire it into a Floodlight, or into anything a switch can control (up to 255 parts).

docs.title: Example: an outpost light
docs.text:
1. Place 2 Solar Panels in the open and wire both into a level 1 Charge Controller.
  2. Wire the Charge Controller into a Mega Battery Bank. A Mega Battery or Rechargeable in the slot is optional reserve power.
  3. Wire the Bank into an Inverter.
  4. Wire the Inverter into a Floodlight, and a Light Sensor into the same Floodlight.

On a clear day the panels make 30 charge. The Floodlight uses 1 charge a night, so the outpost stays lit with plenty to spare for a Charger or a Teleport Pad (1 charge per jump, see Remote Control).

docs.title: Remote Control
docs.text:
Drive and work your creations without sitting in them. A Remote Controller is a driver seat nobody sits in: build it into a creation, aim a handheld Remote at it and you steer with WASD and work its parts with the hotbar from outside. Remote Cameras let you watch from the creation itself, and a Remote Station lets you drive from any empty chair. The same family of parts includes Wireless Transmitters and Receivers (logic signals with no wire between them) and Teleport Pads (jump between pads on the same channel, anywhere in the world).

At a glance

  • Remote Controller: 5 levels, 6 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 connections, upgraded with Component Kits like a Driver Seat.
  • Remote: aim within 7.5 m and press Create to take control. Right-click reconnects to your last controller from any distance.
  • Kept loaded: while you drive, the 3 x 3 map cells around the controller (192 x 192 m) stay loaded, and for 10 seconds after you let go.
  • Remote Cameras: up to 4 per controller. Jump cycles through them.
  • Wireless: 20 channels. Both ends have to be in a loaded part of the world.
  • Teleport Pads: 20 channels, any number of pads per channel. Each jump costs 1 charge from a wired Inverter, or 1 Battery from your inventory.
  • How to get them: all are Craftbot recipes unlocked by Traveling Trader blueprints.

docs.title: How to get them
docs.text:
Every part on this page is built in the Craftbot, but only after the party owns its blueprint from the Traveling Trader. A blueprint unlocks its recipes for the whole party. Rarer blueprints need more trader reputation (see the trader page).

Item Blueprint Rarity Price Needs first Remote Controller (level 1) + Remote Remote Control Rare 144 scrip - Remote Camera Remote Camera Rare 144 scrip Remote Control Wireless Transmitter + Receiver Wireless Link Uncommon 72 scrip - Teleport Pad Teleport Pad Legendary 300 scrip -

Craftbot recipes:

Item Ingredients Craft time Remote Controller 1 Circuit Board, 2 Component Kits, 4 Metal Blocks 20 s Remote 2 Circuit Boards, 1 Battery, 2 Component Kits 20 s Remote Camera 1 Circuit Board, 1 Component Kit, 2 Metal Blocks 15 s Wireless Transmitter 1 Circuit Board, 1 Component Kit, 1 Battery 15 s Wireless Receiver 1 Circuit Board, 1 Component Kit, 2 Metal Blocks 15 s Teleport Pad 4 Circuit Boards, 3 Batteries, 8 Component Kits, 20 Metal Blocks 60 s

Only level 1 of the Remote Controller is crafted. Higher levels come from upgrading it (below). See also Recipes and Items.

docs.title: Remote Controller
docs.text:
Wire it exactly like a Driver Seat: engines, steering bearings, pistons and hotbar parts (thrusters, drills, switches and so on). Nobody can sit in it. Instead, a player with a Remote takes control of it and their input drives the creation.

Press Tinker on it to open the upgrade window. Upgrades cost Component Kits and follow the same steps as the vanilla Driver Seat:

Level Connections Cost to reach this level Extra 1 6 (crafted) 2 8 1 Component Kit 3 12 2 Component Kits 4 16 3 Component Kits 5 20 5 Component Kits Steering joint settings can be adjusted, like a level 5 Driver Seat

Going from level 1 to level 5 costs 11 Component Kits in total.

  • One pilot at a time. The first player to take control drives it. Nobody else's steering counts until that player lets go.
  • The area stays loaded. While someone is driving, the controller keeps the 3 x 3 map cells around it loaded (each cell is 64 m, so 192 x 192 m), moving with the creation. It holds them for another 10 seconds after the pilot lets go, so the creation doesn't freeze mid-move.
  • Up to 4 Remote Cameras can be wired into it. They don't take any of its connections.

Tip

Upgrading keeps your pairing. Right-click reconnect still finds an upgraded controller in the same spot.

docs.title: Remote
docs.text:
The handheld that drives a Remote Controller. Equip it from the hotbar.

Control What it does Aim at a controller (within 7.5 m) + Create Take control. This also pairs the controller with you. W A S D Drive and steer, like sitting in the seat Sprint Sprint, as in a seat 1 - 0 Press the controller's hotbar slots Create / Attack Also press hotbar slots 1 and 2, as in a normal seat Jump Cycle through the controller's Remote Cameras and back to your own view Use Let go. Putting the Remote away also lets go. Attack (right-click) while not aiming at a controller Reconnect to your paired controller, from any distance

Your character stands still while you drive.

docs.title: Reconnecting from far away
docs.text:
The game remembers the last controller each player took control of, and that pairing is saved with the world. Right-click with the Remote (not aimed at a controller) to reconnect:

  • If the controller is loaded, you connect straight away.
  • If it isn't, you see "Remote: waking up controller..." and the area around its last known spot is loaded. When it shows up you're connected. It gets 15 seconds to show up.
  • If it doesn't show up in time, or it was picked up or destroyed, you get "Remote: controller is gone" and the pairing is cleared. Take control of a controller again to pair a new one.
  • With no controller paired yet you get "Remote: no controller paired yet".

Warning

The last known spot is updated while the controller is being driven and whenever it is loaded. A creation that was moved some other way while you weren't around may not be where the Remote expects it.

docs.title: Remote Station
docs.text:
Sit in any vanilla seat (Seat, Saddle, Driver Seat, Driver Saddle or Gyro Seat) that has nothing wired to it: no hotbar parts and no bearings or pistons. If you have a Remote anywhere in your inventory you see "Remote Station - press Create to take control of your Remote Controller".

  • Press Create (or 1) to take control of your paired controller. If it isn't loaded, it is woken up the same way as the Remote's reconnect.
  • You don't need the Remote in your hand, only in your inventory.
  • The seat's hotbar is hidden and the controller's is shown while you drive. WASD, the hotbar, Jump for cameras and Use all work as with the handheld Remote.
  • Use lets go of the controller and keeps you seated. Press Use again to stand up.
  • Taking control with the Remote while you're sitting (aiming it, or right-click reconnect) also drives from the seat.

Tip

A seat that has anything wired to it works as a normal seat, and Create is left to it. Use a spare, unwired chair as your station.

docs.title: Remote Cameras
docs.text:
A camera for remote-controlled creations.

  • Wiring: wire from the camera into the Remote Controller (camera first, then the controller). Each camera has one output; a controller takes up to 4 cameras.
  • Facing: the camera looks out of its front face, the same way a mounted gun fires.
  • Switching views: while driving, press Jump. The view cycles Camera 1, Camera 2, ... and then back to your own view ("Your view"). With no camera wired, Jump tells you "No Remote Camera wired to this controller".
  • Letting go of the controller always returns you to your own view.

docs.title: Wireless Transmitter and Receiver
docs.text:
A logic signal with no wire in between. Transmitters and receivers pair by channel: there is no linking step. Set both to the same channel and they're connected.

Transmitter Receiver Wire into it Up to 10 logic inputs: buttons, switches, logic gates, sensors, seat hotbar slots Nothing Wire out of it Nothing Up to 255 outputs: engines, doors, lights, logic, anything a switch can drive On when Any part wired into it is on Any Transmitter on its channel is on
  • Channels: 1 to 20. New parts start on channel 1. Use goes to the next channel and Tinker to the previous one, wrapping around (20 goes to 1). Look at the part to see its channel.
  • Several transmitters on one channel act like an OR gate: the receivers are on while any of them is on.
  • Range: no distance limit, but both ends have to be in a loaded part of the world, near a player. A transmitter in an unloaded area counts as off.
  • Channels are shared by everyone in the world. In multiplayer, agree on channels so you don't drive each other's receivers.

docs.title: Teleport Pads
docs.text:
Pads on the same channel are linked, wherever they are in the world, even in areas nobody has loaded.

  • Channels: 1 to 20, new pads start on channel 1. Tinker goes to the next channel, crouch + Tinker to the previous one.
  • Teleport: press Use on a pad to jump to the next pad on its channel. Two pads on a channel work as a pair. With three or more, each jump goes on to the next pad in a fixed order, so you cycle through them all.
  • No other pad on the channel: "No other Teleport Pad on channel N".
  • What teleports: only the player who used the pad. Vehicles, creations and items stay behind.
  • Cooldown: none. You can jump again as soon as you arrive.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Each jump costs 1 charge:

  1. From an Inverter wired into the pad, if it has charge (see Power). A pad takes up to 2 wires, and only from Inverters.
  2. Otherwise 1 Battery from your inventory.
  3. With neither: "Teleporting needs 1 charge from wired power, or a battery", and you stay put.

In a world with unlimited inventory, jumps without wired power are free.

Warning

If a pad was picked up or destroyed while nobody was near it, the other pads still think it's there. Jumping to it lands you where it used to be, and after a few seconds you get "The Teleport Pad here is gone - link removed". It is then dropped from the channel.

Tip

Wire the pad at your main base to an Inverter on a solar-charged Mega Battery Bank and the jumps out cost nothing from your pockets. A pad at a far outpost with no power still works: that jump takes a Battery.

docs.title: Scannerbot
docs.text:
The Scannerbot is Survival's flying drone. It patrols the roads at night, scans for players, and hunts them down with homing missiles. It's part of the base game, and Survival Frontier leaves it working as normal, but it adds one thing: the host can switch the Scannerbot off for their world, and back on, with a chat command. Nothing in the story needs the drone, so turning it off doesn't block your progress.

At a glance

  • A flying missile drone from the base game. It's on by default, just like vanilla.
  • Only comes out at night, in the overworld, and only after a point early in the story.
  • It can't be damaged. Weapons, hammers and explosions don't hurt it.
  • Type /scannerbot to see whether it's on in this world.
  • Host only: /scannerbot off removes it from the world, and /scannerbot on brings it back. The setting is saved with the world.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Night patrols. After dark the Scannerbot flies out along the roads, scanning as it goes. It doesn't come out in the day.
  • Hunting. It keeps track of where players have been. Some nights it goes hunting: it moves in close to a player and attacks with homing missiles.
  • More aggressive at first. Its first few hunts happen whatever you do. After that, it waits more than a full day-night cycle between hunts.
  • Overworld only. It doesn't follow you into other worlds.

docs.title: Fighting it
docs.text:
You can't destroy the Scannerbot. Shots and melee hits only spark off it, and explosions do nothing.

Your options are to avoid it:

  • Stay off the roads at night, since that's where it patrols.
  • Or turn it off for your world (below).

docs.title: Turning it on or off
docs.text:
Command Who What it does /scannerbot anyone Says whether the Scannerbot is ON or OFF in this world /scannerbot off host Turns it off. It won't appear in this world any more, and a drone that's flying right now is removed /scannerbot on host Turns it back on. It patrols the roads at night again
  • The setting is saved with the world, so it stays the way you left it after a reload.
  • It's on in every world until the host turns it off.
  • When the host changes it, every player is told who changed it, for example "Alex turned the Scannerbot OFF".
  • If a player who isn't the host tries to change it, they get "Only the host can turn the Scannerbot on or off."
  • When you turn it back on, the base game starts a new drone the next time it would normally appear.

Tip

Turning the Scannerbot off doesn't stop the story, quests or other enemies. It only removes the flying drone.

See Chat commands for every Survival Frontier command.

docs.title: Scrapper
docs.text:
The Scrapper breaks crafted parts back down into 80% of the materials they were made from. Put items in, and a few seconds later the materials are sent down a vacuum pipe into a chest. Which materials come back is random, but you never get more of any one than the recipe used. Items it can't break down pass straight through untouched, so it never jams.

At a glance

  • Returns 80% of a recipe's materials, rounded down (always at least 1).
  • 3 seconds per input stack, 5 input slots.
  • Needs a chest connected by a vacuum pipe. With no piped chest it won't start.
  • Items with no recipe pass through to the chest unchanged.
  • How to get it: a Traveling Trader blueprint (Uncommon, 72 scrip, Customer reputation), then craft it at the Craftbot.

docs.title: Getting a Scrapper
docs.text:
The Scrapper's recipe is a blueprint sold by the Traveling Trader. Buy it once and the whole party can craft Scrappers.

Blueprint Rarity Price Needs Scrapper Uncommon 72 Frontier Scrip Customer reputation (60 scrip spent with him) Crafted at Ingredients Time Craftbot 30 × Metal Block, 5 × Component Kit, 2 × Circuit Board 20 s

The Scrapper is 5 × 3 × 4 blocks.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
1. Place the Scrapper.
  2. Connect a chest to it with vacuum pipes. Any of the Scrapper's three pipe rings works. You can pipe in more than one chest.
  3. Press Use on the Scrapper to open its input and drop items in.

Look at the Scrapper to see what it's doing:

Status Meaning idle Nothing to scrap scrapping... N s Working on a stack connect a chest with a vacuum pipe No piped chest: it won't start piped chest full Every piped chest is full. It waits and tries again each second. Nothing is lost

It works through one stack at a time and scraps the whole stack in one go. You'll see the materials fly down the pipe into the chest.

docs.title: What you get back
docs.text:
For each item, the Scrapper looks up its recipe and adds up all the ingredients. You get 80% of that total, rounded down, and always at least 1. Those units are then drawn at random from the recipe's ingredients, like cards from a deck, so you never get more of one ingredient than the recipe took.

Example Recipe uses You get back 1 Scrapper 37 (30 Metal Block, 5 Component Kit, 2 Circuit Board) 29 of those, mixed at random 1 Pipe Coupler 25 (20 Metal Block, 2 Circuit Board, 2 Glue, 1 Component Kit) 20, mixed at random 1 Scythe 4 (2 Wood Block, 2 Metal Block) 3, mixed at random

If an item can be crafted in more than one place, the cheapest recipe counts, so scrapping never pays more than crafting cost.

docs.title: Recipes that make several items
docs.text:
Some recipes make several items at once (Carbon Pipes come 10 at a time, for example). These only scrap as whole batches: you need the full amount in one stack. Any leftover too small for a batch passes through untouched.

You put in Recipe Result 10 Carbon Pipes 3 Metal Block + 1 Component Kit makes 10 3 units back (80% of 4, rounded down) 15 Carbon Pipes the same 1 batch scrapped (3 units), 5 pipes come out unchanged 7 Carbon Pipes the same not a whole batch: all 7 come out unchanged

docs.title: What it won't break down
docs.text:
The Scrapper only uses Craftbot and Workbench recipes. Anything else goes through to the chest untouched:

  • items with no recipe, such as raw materials you've harvested, loot-only items and Backpack Expansions
  • food and dishes cooked at the Cookbot or Campfire
  • outfits from the Dressbot
  • refined materials from the Refinery
  • items whose only recipe is at a trader

Older Scrappers

Scrappers placed before the pipe update have a second, old output bin. If there's anything in it, it's emptied into the piped chest before anything new is scrapped.

docs.title: Craftbot cancel buttons
docs.text:
While a Craftbot window is open, a strip of red CANCEL buttons sits between the window and your hotbar, one under each crafting slot that's in use.

  • Cancel takes that craft off the queue and gives all its ingredients back to the inventory of whoever clicked.
  • If your inventory can't hold them, you get an inventory full message and the craft stays queued.
  • A repeating craft that's only waiting for materials has nothing to refund. Cancelling it just takes it off the queue and stops it pulling from pipes.
  • Finished crafts have no button. Collect them as usual.
  • Empty and locked slots have no button either.

The strip fits 16:9, 16:10, 21:9 and 4:3 screens. It replaced the old crouch + Use Craft Queue window (from 1.3.0, crouch + Use on a Craftbot no longer opens it).

docs.title: Traveling Trader
docs.text:
The Traveling Trader flies a scrap airship (the Tug) around the frontier and sets down somewhere new every few in-game days. Next to the Tug he puts up his Stall, and there you can spend the Frontier Scrip you earn from contracts on blueprints (recipe unlocks for the whole party), Backpack Expansions, his own dish recipes, and Outpost Boards. The more scrip your party spends with him, the better his reputation with you gets, and the better the stock he will sell you.

At a glance

  • He camps 300 m to 1.5 km from the Hideout's Contract Board, in a random direction.
  • He stays 2 to 3 in-game days (about 48 to 72 minutes of play), then moves on. He won't pack up while anyone is within 64 m of the camp.
  • An orange marker on the map and compass shows where he is. Type /trader in chat for his location and your reputation.
  • You pay only in Frontier Scrip, and it has to be in the buyer's own inventory.
  • Each blueprint or recipe is bought once for the whole party.
  • Reputation counts the party's lifetime scrip spent with him: Stranger (0), Customer (60), Regular (250), Partner (600).
  • He sells 20 blueprints, 11 dish recipes, Backpack Expansions (800 scrip, from Partner) and up to 6 Outpost Boards (from Frontier Standing rank 3).

docs.title: Where he camps
docs.text:
When it's time to move, the trader picks a random spot between 300 m and 1,500 m from the Hideout's Contract Board. If the Hideout board hasn't been found yet, he measures from any Contract Board the party knows. He never camps on a lake.

When he arrives, every player gets a message such as "The Traveling Trader has set up camp about 900 m north-east of the Hideout". The distance is rounded to 10 m, or shown in km past 1,000 m.

The camp is only built when a player comes within 150 m of the spot. He then looks up to 60 m around it for dry, fairly flat ground and puts the Tug, the Stall and himself there. If there's no dry ground nearby, the site shifts 125 to 250 m further on and he tries again. Because of this, the camp may sit a little off the place he first named.

Brand-new worlds

He only appears once the game knows where a Contract Board is, so in a new world he turns up shortly after the Hideout area has loaded. Until then, /trader says "Nobody has seen the Traveling Trader yet - visit the Contract Board at the Hideout".

docs.title: Map marker and /trader
docs.text:
An orange quest marker hangs over the camp. It also shows on your compass and moves whenever he does.

Type /trader in chat to see:

  • where he's camped (for example "about 1.2 km south-west of the Hideout - follow the orange marker")
  • your party's reputation and how much scrip you've spent with him in total

See Chat commands for the other commands.

docs.title: How long he stays
docs.text:
He stays 2 to 3 in-game days at each camp. The exact time is random within that range. One in-game day is 24 minutes, so that's about 48 to 72 minutes of play. The timer only runs while the game is running.

The Stall window's footer shows how long is left ("Packing up and moving on in ..."). When time runs out he waits until nobody is within 64 m of the camp, so he never leaves while you're shopping. Then he moves to a new spot. If you come across an old Tug or Stall from an earlier camp, it packs itself up. Only the current camp sells anything.

docs.title: The Stall
docs.text: Walk up to the Stall or to the trader himself and press Use to open the shop. The Tug is scenery only. The trader waves when you open the window, makes a deal gesture when you buy and nods goodbye when you close it.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
• Header: your reputation level, a 10-segment bar towards the next level, and how much more scrip you need plus what it unlocks (for example "190 more scrip to Regular: Rare blueprints"). It also shows how much scrip you're carrying.
  • Tabs: Blueprints, Recipes and Gear. Each tab label shows how many items in it the party hasn't bought yet.
  • Cards: 12 per page (4 x 3), with page arrows when a tab has more. Each card shows:
    • the price, in gold if you can afford it and red if you can't
    • Locked if you can't buy it yet
    • Owned if the party already has it
  • Detail panel: a 3D preview, the grade (rarity, cooking tier or Gear), a description, and the list of everything a blueprint unlocks. A locked item says what unlocks it.

docs.title: Buying
docs.text:
1. Pick a card.
  2. Press Buy. The button changes to Confirm purchase.
  3. Press it again within 3 seconds to buy.

The scrip comes out of your own inventory, not a chest. If you don't have enough, the button says "Need N more scrip". Blueprints and recipes unlock straight away for everyone in the party, and everyone sees " bought the ... blueprint for the party". Gear goes into the buyer's inventory, so you need a free slot.

Carry your scrip

The Stall only counts the scrip in the inventory of the player pressing Buy. Scrip in a chest at base doesn't count, and you can't combine scrip from several players for one purchase. Hand it to one player first.

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
Your reputation with the trader is the party's lifetime scrip spent at his Stall. Every purchase counts: blueprints, dish recipes, Backpack Expansions and Outpost Boards. Reputation never goes down.

Level Lifetime scrip spent Unlocks for sale Stranger 0 Common blueprints Customer 60 Uncommon blueprints Regular 250 Rare blueprints Partner 600 Legendary blueprints and Backpack Expansions

Reputation belongs to the whole party (the world), not to each player. Anyone's purchases raise it for everyone. When you reach a new level, everyone gets a message such as "The Traveling Trader now counts you as a Regular - Rare blueprints are for sale".

Locked items stay on show, so you can see what's coming. Dish recipes and Outpost Boards don't need any reputation (see below).

docs.title: Blueprints
docs.text:
A blueprint unlocks one or more crafting recipes for the whole party, permanently. Prices depend on rarity:

Rarity Price Reputation needed Common 30 Stranger Uncommon 72 Customer Rare 144 Regular Legendary 300 Partner

docs.title: Trader dish recipes
docs.text:
The Recipes tab sells the trader's own dishes. You can't research these at the Cookbot like other dishes. You can only buy them, and each is bought once for the whole party. See Kitchen for how cooking and research work.

They don't need any reputation. Instead, a trader dish unlocks for sale once the party has researched any other dish of the same tier. Until then it shows "Research a dish first". All 11 cost 1,104 scrip together. Trader dishes are a step above the other dishes of their tier:

  • they restore 5 more health: 65 / 85 / 97 / 103 against 60 / 80 / 92 / 98 for tiers 1 to 4
  • their buffs last 20% longer

The dish reference has the full stats and ingredients.

docs.title: Backpack Expansion
docs.text:
• Price: 800 scrip
  • Needs: Partner reputation

A Backpack Expansion permanently adds a row of 10 slots to the inventory of whoever uses it, up to 10 extra rows per player. Unlike blueprints it's an item: it goes into the buyer's inventory, and you can buy as many as you like. Hand one to a teammate if you want. See Backpack for how to use one. Expansions can also turn up as rare contract rewards at the top Frontier Standing.

docs.title: Outpost Board
docs.text:
An Outpost Board is a Contract Board you set up yourself out on the frontier. It has to stand at least 1.5 km from every other Contract Board, on solid ground (not on a vehicle). Once it opens, new contracts are posted around it as well as around the Hideout. See Contracts.

  • Needs: Frontier Standing rank 3 (from finishing contracts). It needs no trader reputation.
  • Limit: 6 per party. After that the card says "No more Outpost Boards".
  • Price: goes up by 200 scrip with each board the party buys:
Board 1st 2nd 3rd 4th 5th 6th Price 400 600 800 1,000 1,200 1,400

All six cost 5,400 scrip together.

docs.title: Earning scrip
docs.text: Frontier Scrip is the reward for finishing contracts from the Contract Boards. Higher Frontier Standing brings better-paying contracts. See Contracts for how to earn it.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text:
Everything at the trader is shared by the party, except the scrip you pay with:

Shared by the party Per player Camp location, timer and map marker The scrip used for a purchase (the buyer's inventory) Reputation (lifetime spend) Where a bought Backpack Expansion or Outpost Board goes (the buyer's inventory) Every blueprint and dish recipe bought Backpack rows (each player's own, up to 10) Outpost Boards bought (and so their price and the cap of 6)
  • Any player can buy, and everyone sees the purchase and any reputation level-up announced in chat.
  • The trader stays put as long as any player is within 64 m.

docs.title: Old worlds and new worlds
docs.text:
• New worlds: none of the trader's machines and gadgets are known at the start. You get the Floodlight, Solar Panel, Scrapper, Teleport Pad and the rest by buying their blueprints from him.
  • Worlds from before the trader was added: any of those recipes the world had already unlocked stay unlocked, because unlocks are saved with the world. They show as Owned at the Stall, and the party only needs to buy the ones it never had.
  • The trader dish recipes were never researchable, so every world buys them from him.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Fast track to Partner

Every purchase counts towards reputation, dishes and Outpost Boards included. Buying all five Common blueprints (150 scrip) gets you past Customer. Add a few Uncommons, or the early dish recipes, to reach Regular (250). Buying all the Common and Uncommon blueprints comes to 726 scrip, which is enough for Partner (600) by itself.

Plan blueprint chains

The Charge Controller and Inverter need the Solar Panel. The Charger needs the Rechargeable Battery, the Remote Camera needs the Remote Control, the Throttle Thruster needs Signal Parts, and the Mega Battery Bank needs the Mega Battery. Buy the base blueprint first so its follow-ups are ready when your reputation catches up.

Research one dish per tier

You only need to research one ordinary dish of a tier at the Cookbot to open all of the trader's dishes for that tier. Their extra health and longer buffs make them some of the best food in the game for their tier.

Shop before he leaves

Check the footer of the Stall window for how long he's staying. If the timer is about to run out, he still won't leave while someone is within 64 m. Once you walk away he'll move on, and he can land up to 1.5 km away.

Put an outpost near his range

His camps are measured from the Hideout, but contracts are posted around every open board. An Outpost Board set up along a route you travel often gives you a place to hand in contracts and pick up new ones on the way.
